paragraphs.heading: Learning about the whole from a part
paragraphs.text: Statisticians often want to know something about a whole population, such as the average height of everyone in a country. Instead of measuring everyone, they can measure a sample, a subset drawn from that population. Numbers worked out from the sample, such as its mean, are called estimators. The true values for the whole population are called parameters.

paragraphs.heading: The gap called sampling error
paragraphs.text: Because a sample leaves out some members of the population, its numbers generally do not match the population's exactly. The difference between a sample statistic and the true population value is called the sampling error. Measure the heights of a thousand people out of a million, and their average will usually not equal the average of all million. The true value is usually unknown, so the error cannot be measured exactly, but it can often be estimated.

paragraphs.heading: Bias makes things worse
paragraphs.text: A truly random sample gives every member of the population the same chance of being picked. Getting this wrong causes sampling bias, which can push the error a long way in one direction. Imagine trying to find the average height of all humans by measuring people in just one country; the answer could be far too high or far too low. In practice, many factors such as age, gender or country can skew a sample, and none of them should be allowed to shape who gets chosen.

paragraphs.heading: Chance never fully goes away
paragraphs.text: Even a perfectly unbiased sample still carries some error from chance alone. If you averaged the heights of just two or three people, the result would swing wildly from one try to the next. A larger sample generally makes the likely error smaller. But bigger samples cost more, and that cost can be too high, so methods for choosing a sample size weigh the expected accuracy against the expected cost.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the spread
paragraphs.text: A statistic such as an average or a percentage will vary from one sample to another. By comparing many samples, or by splitting one large sample into smaller pieces, you can see how much the results spread out. That spread is used to estimate the standard error. Another general way to estimate sampling error is a technique called bootstrapping.

paragraphs.heading: A different use in genetics
paragraphs.text: In genetics, the phrase sampling error has been used in a related but quite different sense. When a disaster or a migration shrinks a population sharply, as in the bottleneck or founder effect, the survivors may not fairly represent the original group. Some gene variants then become more or less common. This is a source of genetic drift, even though it is not an error in the statistical sense.
